# OPCH Technical Analysis Report — as of 2026-10-09

## Headline: A violent repricing, not a trend

The dominant feature of OPCH's chart is a single event: on **2026-10-06** the stock jumped from a 2026-10-05 close of **$23.37** to a close of **$31.00** — roughly **+33% overnight** — on **65.08M shares**, more than 30x the typical ~1.5–2M daily volume of the prior three months. This is the signature of a fundamental catalyst (earnings, guidance, M&A speculation, or a major contract/regulatory event), not an organic trend. Since then the stock has gone nearly dead-flat: closes of 31.00 → 31.01 → 31.05 → **31.07** on 10-09, with intraday ranges collapsing to a few cents and volume decaying each day (65M → 19.4M → 9.7M → 6.2M). That is a **price-lock / consolidation at the new level**, the kind of tape you often see when a deal price or a re-rated equilibrium is anchoring trading.

## Pre-event context (July → early October)

- July was strong: OPCH rallied from ~$21.6 to a peak of **$24.96 intraday on 2026-07-29** (earnings-type volume spike: 5.3M shares on 07-29, 5.1M on 07-30).
- August–September were a slow bleed: price chopped in a $22.3–$24.9 band with a downward drift, bottoming at **$22.49 on 2026-09-30**. RSI sat in a weak 37–50 range and MACD was negative through late September — classic distribution/fade conditions.
- The 10-05 session ($22.45→$23.37, 2.8M shares) already showed pre-event strength; the 10-06 gap completed the move.

## Indicator read (verified snapshot, 2026-10-09)

- **Close 31.07 vs 50 SMA 24.23 (+28%) and 200 SMA 26.42 (+18%)**: price is massively extended above both trend benchmarks. The 50 SMA is still catching up and will keep rising mechanically as old ~$23 prints roll off — do not read the rising SMA as fresh buying pressure.
- **10 EMA at 27.47** is ramping steeply toward price but remains ~12% below. Short-term fair-value drag is still well under the market.
- **RSI 83.8** — deep overbought, but this is event-driven overbought, not momentum-chasing overbought. RSI will stay pinned high as long as price holds near $31; it is not a reliable sell signal in a price-lock regime. If the pin breaks, RSI will collapse quickly from extreme levels.
- **MACD 1.60 vs signal 0.65 (histogram +0.96)**: huge bullish crossover and expanding gap — but again, mechanically driven by four days at $31. It confirms the repricing, not future direction.
- **Bollinger: middle 24.94, upper 31.31, lower 18.58.** Price (31.07) is riding just under the upper band after tagging through it on 10-06. The band width (18.58 → 31.31) is enormous — the volatility regime fully reset. Touching the upper band here is descriptive, not a mean-reversion trigger.
- **ATR 0.95 and falling** (from 1.17 on 10-06): volatility is compressing hard post-event. True range on 10-09 was only $0.08 — ATR is still inflated by the gap day and will keep declining.

## Actionable takeaways

- **The $31.00–31.11 zone is the market's verdict** for now. Four consecutive sessions pinned within a ~$0.10 range after a 33% gap strongly suggests an anchored price (deal-like behavior) or an accepted new equilibrium. Breaks of this pin — either direction — are the tradable information.
- **Chasing here is low edge**: price is ~28% above the 50 SMA, ~12% above the 10 EMA, and just under the upper Bollinger band. Mean-reversion risk is asymmetric if the anchor fails; downside air pockets toward the 10 EMA (~27.5) and then the gap origin (~$23.4, the 10-05 close) are the natural magnets.
- **If long from below**: the technical stop structure argues for using the pin's low (~$31.00 area) or the 10-06 gap level as the line; a break back into the $23–24 gap zone would void the repricing thesis entirely.
- **If flat**: the clean setups are (a) a confirmed breakout above ~$31.11 with volume re-expansion, or (b) a failed pin / gap-fill toward $27 (10 EMA) or $23.5. Sideways scalping inside $31.00–31.11 has near-zero range to harvest.
- **Volume is the tell**: each day's halving of volume supports consolidation rather than distribution; renewed multi-million-share selling would be the first warning the anchor is breaking.

## Caveats

- Technicals are nearly useless for *why* this moved — a 33% one-day reprice on 65M shares is a news/event artifact. Any position here should be sized against headline risk, not indicator signals.
- All lagging indicators (SMAs, Bollinger middle) are still ingesting the gap; their values will shift mechanically over the next ~20 sessions.

## Key Points Table

| Last close | $31.07 | Pinned for 4 straight sessions $31.00–31.07 |
| Event | 2026-10-06 gap: $23.37 → $31.00 (~+33%) on 65M shares | Fundamental repricing; not trend-driven |
| 10 EMA | 27.47 | ~12% below price; first downside magnet on weakness |

# OPCH — Fundamental Research Report
Instrument: OPCH — Option Care Health, Inc.
Point-in-time: 2026-10-09. All figures below are from SEC EDGAR facts filed on or before that date, in USD millions unless noted.

## Data availability and caveats
- Company profile, market cap, valuation multiples and 52-week range were withheld by the vendor for this date, so this report is built strictly from filed financial statements.
- Insider transactions were withheld for this date; no insider signal can be reported.
- The latest statement period available is the quarter ended 2026-03-31. No material new fundamental filing is visible in the data for the week ending 2026-10-09 itself.

## Company profile
Option Care Health is a U.S. provider of home and alternate-site infusion therapy services. Revenue scale (~$1.35B in the latest quarter) is consistent with one of the largest independent infusion providers in the U.S. The business is reimbursement-driven: growth depends on therapy mix, referral volumes, and payer rates, while profitability depends on drug procurement costs and labor efficiency.

## Latest quarter (Q1 2026, ended 2026-03-31)
- Revenue: $1,351M — continued large-scale top line; down sequentially from the ~$1,435M prior-quarter level but up versus the ~$1,227M reported a year earlier (roughly +10% y/y), consistent with steady demand in home infusion.
- Gross profit: $262M — gross margin ~19.4%, in line with the company's structural ~19–21% band; margins are thin and highly sensitive to drug cost and mix.
- Operating income: $73M — operating margin ~5.4%, near the low end of the recent ~$73–85M quarterly range.
- Net income: $45M; diluted EPS $0.29 — modestly below the strongest recent quarters (~$0.31–0.32 EPS) but consistent with a profitable, stable earnings base.
- Operating cash flow: -$12M — negative in Q1, matching the company's recurring pattern of weak/negative Q1 operating cash flow followed by positive later quarters (e.g., ~-$7M in Q1 2025, then strongly positive cumulative flows). This looks seasonal (working-capital timing) rather than a new deterioration, but it is worth confirming when the Q2/Q3 2026 filings appear.
- Investing cash flow: -$9M; capital expenditure ~$9M — capex remains light (~0.7% of quarterly revenue), a favorable cash-conversion characteristic.
- Financing cash flow: -$34M — continued net financing outflows (debt service/repayment and/or buybacks), consistent with recent quarters.

## Balance sheet (2026-03-31)
- Total assets: $3,380M; total liabilities: $2,029M; stockholders' equity: $1,351M.
- Liabilities are ~60% of assets; liabilities-to-equity ≈ 1.5x — leveraged but stable, with equity having rebuilt steadily from ~$922M at end-2020 to ~$1,351M.
- Current assets: $1,195M vs. current liabilities: $730M → current ratio ≈ 1.64 — adequate short-term liquidity.
- Cash and equivalents: $177M — thin relative to $730M of current liabilities; liquidity depends on ongoing operating cash generation and revolver capacity, so the seasonal Q1 cash burn is a real (if familiar) watch item.

## Financial history and trajectory
- Revenue has compounded from ~$460–500M per quarter in 2019 to ~$1.35–1.44B recently — roughly tripling over six years, driven by organic growth plus acquisitions.
- The earnings base turned sustainably positive around 2022–2023 (net income roughly $30–56M per quarter) after years of losses and restructuring-era volatility (e.g., the ~$245M net loss in 2015).
- Annualized operating cash generation in recent years has been strong (cumulative figures exceeded $200–300M by Q3 of recent years), supporting gradual deleveraging of a balance sheet that carries ~$2.0B of liabilities.
- Book equity per the latest balance (~$1.35B) implies the market is valuing the ongoing earnings/cash-flow stream well above book, typical for a scaled services provider — but note valuation multiples themselves were not available for this date.

## Actionable takeaways for traders
- Thesis support: durable double-digit-ish revenue scale-up, stable ~19–20% gross margins, consistent positive net income (~$45–55M/quarter) and ~$0.29–0.32 quarterly EPS — fundamentals back a "steady compounder" profile rather than a high-growth story.

Bull Analyst: # Bull Case for OPCH — Option Care Health

Let me open this debate by naming the elephant in the room, because it's the best possible news for bulls: **this stock just got a signed, definitive $32.05 all-cash buyout from McKesson and Clayton Dubilier & Rice — roughly $5.8B enterprise value, a ~37% premium to where it traded five days ago.** Every other argument in this debate runs through that fact.

## 1. The catalyst is not speculation — it's a signed deal

Bears will talk about overbought RSI and "chasing." Here's the reframe: the market isn't pricing momentum, it's pricing a **contracted outcome**. A strategic buyer with deep industry knowledge — McKesson, one of the largest healthcare distributors on the planet — looked at Option Care's books and decided the business was worth $32.05 in cash, plus CD&R's private equity validation on top. Two sophisticated, non-overlapping buyer types (strategic + financial sponsor) agreed on value. That is the strongest third-party fundamental endorsement a mid-cap can get.

The four-day pin at $31.00–$31.07 on decaying volume isn't weakness — it's the market accepting the deal price as the anchor. With the stock at $31.07, there's ~3% of spread left to $32.05 that compresses toward zero as closing milestones hit (shareholder vote, HSR/regulatory clearance). That's a defined, near-term return uncorrelated with the broader tape.

## 2. The fundamentals were already working before the deal

Strip away the event and the underlying business is a steady compounder:

- **Revenue ~3x'd since 2019** — from ~$460–500M/quarter to ~$1.35B, with Q1 2026 still growing ~+10% y/y. That's durable, reimbursement-driven demand in home infusion — a structurally growing niche as care shifts out of hospitals.
- **Consistently profitable since 2022–23**: ~$45M net income, $0.29 diluted EPS last quarter, in a stable earnings band.
- **Asset-light**: capex ~0.7% of revenue. This is a cash-generation model, not a capital sink.
- **Defensible positioning**: largest independent home/alternate-site infusion provider in the US. Scale in drug procurement, nursing networks, and payer contracts is the moat — and it's exactly what a buyer like McKesson covets.

Smart money didn't buy a story — it bought verified cash flows at a 37% premium. That reprices the floor, not just the ceiling.

## 3. Preempting the bear arguments

**"It's overbought — RSI 83.8."** Agreed, and irrelevant. The technical report itself says it: this is event-driven overbought in a price-lock regime, not momentum chasing. RSI is pinned because price is pinned to a deal anchor. You don't fade a signed merger on RSI.

**"Downside if the deal breaks — back to $23."** That's the real bear case, and it's fair. But weigh it honestly: (a) it's a definitive agreement, not a rumor; (b) cash deal, no financing-contingency complexity typical of LBO blowups; (c) McKesson's strategic stake logic and CD&R's diligence both de-risk completion; (d) even the "break" scenario lands you back at a company growing 10% y/y with stable margins that screened as undervalued pre-deal (@Tickrtrends flagged it >25% below fair value *before* the bid). The downside floor is a business that was already cheap.

**"Macro headwinds — rates at 3-year highs."** For a standalone company relying on debt-funded roll-ups, sure. But the deal structure moves that risk to the buyers' balance sheets, and falling oil (Iran de-escalation) directly eases OPCH's nurse-travel and delivery cost structure — a quiet margin tailwind.

**"Only 3% left — is the trade even worth it?"** For a trader, ~3% to a contracted cash price over a closing timeline is an attractive annualized arb yield with a defined catalyst path. For an investor, the deal itself is the bull thesis validated: the market spent months mispricing this business at $23, and it took $5.8B of conviction capital to correct it. If you were waiting for proof the fundamentals were sound, McKesson just wrote the proof.

## 4. The verdict

Bull score here isn't about blue-sky upside — it's about **asymmetry with an anchor**. Up side: $32.05 cash, spread compressing on each milestone. Down side: a break scenario back to a fundamentals-supported ~$23–24 that bears themselves have to admit was the *undervalued* price. Base case probability strongly favors completion, sentiment is unanimously event-positive with zero bearish messages in the live feed, and the volume signature says consolidation, not distribution.

The bear will have to argue the deal fails. Everything else — overbought indicators, macro noise, thin Q1 cash flow — is decoration around a signed contract. I'll take the contract.

Over to you, Bear — tell me why McKesson and CD&R both got it wrong.

Bear Analyst: # Bear Case for OPCH — You're Not Buying a Stock, You're Buying a Merger Spread

Bull, I'll grant you the framing: this debate is about the deal. But you've mistaken "the deal exists" for "the deal is done," and you've mistaken "the floor is $23" for "the floor is safe." Let me take your own points apart.

## 1. Your asymmetry is upside-down — and your own numbers prove it

You called this "asymmetry with an anchor." Look at the actual payout structure you're endorsing:

- **Upside: ~3%.** $31.07 to $32.05. That's the *entire* remaining return. Finite, contracted, capped.
- **Downside on a break: ~25-26%.** Back to the ~$23.37 pre-deal close — the level the market itself set on October 5th.

That is a roughly **8:1 loss-to-gain ratio**. For this trade to be fair value, the deal needs to close with ~90%+ probability. Cash deals close more often than not — but merger arb desks earn their living precisely because that tail is real, lumpy, and correlated. You're not making a bull case on OPCH; you're underwriting a one-sided insurance policy and calling it conviction. A bet where you risk $8 to win $1 is a bear's argument wearing a bull costume.

And note what the tape is telling you: the spread **isn't compressing**. Four sessions pinned at $31.00–$31.07, still ~$0.98 below deal price. If completion were the near-certainty you describe, arbs would have ground this to $31.80+ already. The market is pricing residual deal risk — and keeping a stubborn ~3% discount says smart money isn't as comfortable as you are.

## 2. "Two sophisticated buyers agreed" — so did the buyers in every busted deal ever signed

McKesson and CD&R agreeing on $32.05 is an endorsement of value, not of certainty. The definitive agreement still has to survive:

- **Regulatory review.** This is a healthcare services consolidation — McKesson taking a stake in the largest independent home-infusion provider is exactly the kind of vertical/horizontal overlap that draws FTC scrutiny in this environment. Extended review means extended time in the pin, and time is the enemy of an overbought, headline-dependent stock.
- **Shareholder and closing conditions** you haven't read — and neither has the StockTwits feed. Nobody in this debate has seen the merger agreement's termination provisions, break fees, or MAC clause. You're treating a contract neither of us has fully parsed as a sure thing.
- **Rate environment working against deal economics.** Your own macro report flags mortgage/funding rates at ~3-year highs with FRED data unavailable. CD&R's side of this is private equity — PE economics are *rate-sensitive by definition*. You can't wave the "higher-for-longer" flag in the macro section and then claim financing risk moved neatly to "the buyers' balance sheet." Buyers with stretched financing math are precisely how signed deals get renegotiated or walked.

## 3. The "undervalued floor" is softer than you admit

You lean on @Tickrtrends' "25% below fair value" screen and the ~$23–24 pre-deal range as a safe landing. Three problems:

- **The pre-deal range was falling, not stable.** Your own technical report: August–September was a "slow bleed," down drift, RSI 37–50, negative MACD, bottoming at $22.49 on 9-30.
